analysis.one_liner: Freezes imports of textiles, clothing, and shoes near 1989 levels to protect US factories and jobs.
analysis.headline: Backed by 250 of 435 House members, the bill died in a Ways and Means subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cap imports of textiles, clothing, and nonrubber shoes at roughly their 1989 levels — textiles at 101% of the prior year, shoes frozen entirely — with only 1% growth allowed each year after. Its stated purpose is to stop factory closings and job losses in US textile, apparel, and footwear plants. It would also bar the President from lowering tariffs on these goods or negotiating them away in trade talks, and would run a one-year pilot auction of textile import licenses, with the money going to the Treasury.
analysis.who_benefits: US textile, apparel, and footwear manufacturers, who would keep a larger share of the American market, and the workers at those plants, whose jobs the bill explicitly aims to protect [S2][S3]. Domestic cotton and wool growers would also benefit from a shielded market for their fiber, a point the bill makes at length in its findings [S3]. Because the import licenses would be auctioned, part of the windfall from scarcity would flow to the Treasury rather than to import quota holders [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: US textile, apparel, and footwear makers and workers

how_it_helps.text: Caps 1990 textile imports at 101% of 1989 volumes and freezes nonrubber footwear imports at their 1989 level, allowing only 1% annual growth for textiles afterward — a hard ceiling where imports had been growing about 10% a year.

Targets job preservation directly: the bill's stated policy is to prevent 'loss of job opportunities' for textile, clothing, and footwear workers, citing a claimed 1.4 million apparel-sector jobs lost and a 45% drop in footwear employment since 1981.
Shields domestic cotton and wool growers from a shrinking market, citing more than $1 billion a year in lost cotton revenue as foreign-made clothing replaced domestic cloth.
Includes a pilot auction of textile import licenses in 1991, so at least part of the quota's scarcity value is captured by the US Treasury instead of being kept by whoever held the import rights.

analysis.who_pays: American consumers, who would pay more for clothing and shoes once import volumes were capped below what the market had been absorbing; the bill would also prevent the President from negotiating any tariff relief on these goods, locking in the higher prices [S3]. Importers and retailers would face tighter supply and would have to bid at auction for the right to bring goods in, and foreign clothing and textile exporters — mostly in developing countries — would lose sales [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: American shoppers; clothing importers and retailers

drawbacks.text: Binding quotas on clothing and shoes mean higher prices for every American household; clothing takes a bigger bite out of low-income budgets, so the cost falls hardest on people the bill's job protection doesn't reach.

The bill handcuffs trade policy: it flatly prohibits the President from cutting textile or footwear duties by any means, or even proposing a cut, going beyond this bill to freeze future trade negotiations on the entire sector.

Allowing only 1% import growth while the domestic market grows about 1% effectively freezes import market share permanently, and the bill itself concedes the limits would breach US trade commitments by requiring the President to negotiate compensation for trading partners under international trade agreements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver real protection to a large, labor-intensive group of domestic factories and their workers, and its license-auction pilot is a genuinely smart touch that returns part of the quota windfall to the Treasury. But the honest trade-off is steep: quotas work by making clothing and shoes scarcer and dearer, so the cost is spread across every shopper, and the per-household hit, while individually modest, adds up to far more than the wages saved — the classic arithmetic of protection. The blanket ban on future tariff negotiations is hard to defend on its own terms, since it locks the sector's high prices in place even if conditions change. This is a bill that helps a particular set of workers and their employers by taxing everyone who gets dressed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with 250 cosponsors but sent to a Ways and Means trade subcommittee that never voted on it, and it died when the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marilyn Lloyd introduced the bill on April 4, 1990, with 250 cosponsors — 194 of the House's 257 Democrats and 56 of its 175 Republicans, a clear majority of the chamber.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and on April 12 sent it to the Subcommittee on Trade.
No hearing, markup, or vote ever followed; the bill sat in subcommittee until the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and it never became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Importers, retailers, foreign clothing and textile exporters, and American shoppers — who avoided higher clothing and shoe prices and kept the tariff-negotiating freeze from taking effect. The domestic textile, apparel, and footwear industries and their workers, despite a House majority's sponsorship, got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Shoppers, retailers, and foreign clothing exporters

for.name: Rep. Marilyn Lloyd
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, an annual effort she led on behalf of textile-district interests.

for.name: 194 of 257 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making up more than three-quarters of the Democratic caucus.

for.name: 56 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, about a third of the Republican caucus.

for.name: Textile, apparel, and footwear manufacturers and textile unions
for.what_they_did: Lobbied for the annual textile-quota bill, which Congress had debated in various forms since the early 1980s.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee, Subcommittee on Trade
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 4, 1990, referred it to the Trade Subcommittee on April 12, and never held a markup or vote; the bill died there.

against.name: Bush administration
against.what_they_did: Opposed textile import-quota legislation and threatened to veto similar bills, standing against the protectionist push.

against.name: Retailers and importers
against.what_they_did: Fought textile import quotas, which would restrict the goods they sell and require them to bid at auction for import licenses.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily bipartisan: 194 of 257 House Democrats and 56 of 175 House Republicans cosponsored, a majority of the full House, yet the bill never reached the floor.

industries.note: The bill would freeze their foreign competition near 1989 volumes, preserving their market share and their workers' jobs. The mechanism for doing so is higher clothing prices for every American consumer, so the industry's gain comes directly at the public's cost.
Footwear imports were already 80% of the US market, and the bill would cap them at 1989 levels with no growth. It would prop up a shrinking domestic industry by raising the price of shoes.

industries.industry: Clothing and shoe importers and retailers
industries.note: Importers would face hard volume caps and would have to buy import licenses at public auction, while retailers would carry less merchandise at higher wholesale cost. Their interest here runs with consumers', who want cheap and plentiful goods.

industries.industry: Foreign textile and apparel exporters (developing countries)
industries.note: Suppliers in more than 165 countries, many of them low-wage garment workers abroad, would lose access to the US market. The bill even requires the President to negotiate compensation to them for the broken trade commitments.

The bill's findings argue that imported clothing contains mostly foreign cotton and has cost US cotton growers over $1 billion a year in revenue. Cutting imports would restore demand for domestic fiber.
